responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

In this issue we are able to return to our project to compare schools of thought through the medium of commentaries upon clinical material. This effort was highly regarded in the first issue even though the commentaries themselves were disagreed with. That was all to the good: it seems to suggest genuine differences of approach. Comment on these commentaries would be worthwhile collecting and we will, if that is forthcoming, make that one feature of a correspondence section. So readers are invited to express their views. Because of the nature of printers' deadlines and publishers' obsessionalities, it is difficult to get letters into the subsequent issue, and in this issue we have reactions to the contents of the first issue - including the clinical commentary.

The comparison of different models is the theme of a large proportion of this issue. Delmonte and Kenny tackle a vast literature of meditation and classify the types into two general forms - the concentrative techniques and the mentally expanding techniques. Meditation has been reviewed by psychoanalytic writers and the present authors enter into the discussion of the most appropriate framework for thinking about meditation, comparing a psychoanalytic model with a behavioural one and a personal construct theory model. Pedder looks at a very different topic-depression - and the progress of psychoanalytic theory of the factors involved. He is impressed with the possible common factor of low self esteem in various non-psychoanalytic models (e.g. Brown's sociological model) which correspond to the psychoanalytic model of impaired internalisation of good experiences and a good internal object that sustains self-esteem.

Introjective problems are also the focus of the clinically oriented paper by Robert May. He discusses and illustrates theories of narcissism. The particular contenders are those of Kernberg and of Kohut. He also makes the interesting point that these American writers are ranged against each other over points which are introduced from European, especially British, psychoanalysis. Kernberg adopts some of the framework evolved by Melanie Klein, while Kohut has looked to the work of Winnicott. Some of the argument over frustrating environment versus innate envy has taken a transatlantic crossing, and is now making a return trip!

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

The policy of the Journal is to provide as wide a spread of interesting material on psychoanalytical psychotherapy as possible. With this overall policy we can therefore include a curiosity like the plea for a reinstatement of Incest which, in the view reported by the French journalist Isobel Domon, is a much maligned activity! It is certainly refreshing to have stated what everyone knows is a profoundly sensual and sexual quality in the contact with the bodies of infants and young children.

Cecilia Clementel-Jones also dwells on an apparent gap in awareness, at least in the literature. She draws attention to the paucity of writing on the experience of being pregnant as a therapist. The pregnant therapist is well known as a phantasy of the patient. What happens when such phantasies meet an obliging reality that confirms them? This is an intensely important area of interest - the boundary between intrapsychic reality (phantasy) and the actual interpersonal (external) reality.

The interpersonal world is no more evident than in large groups, and the furiously chaotic events need urgent space for therapists to recover themselves. Pullen describes in a commendably placid way his work with staff groups, largely untrained in matters unconscious but frighteningly zealous to be therapeutic. The avid wish to therapise and the particular fearfulness of the large group make an explosive mixture, which Pullen dissects calmly and sensitively.

The effective working of the staff team is also the focus of Maurice White's paper on working with delinquent and perverse criminals in a therapeutic community. The defensiveness of the staff in confronting the sadistic and perverse transference that arise and that are acted out in the community, is, he claims, the focus of the most vital therapeutic effort. His aim, in the staff seminars he holds, is to enable the staff to resist being drawn into either sadistic reaction, or excited identifications; and to bring these personal reactions into a verbal discourse, at least within the staff group.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary II

[In this section a short piece of clinical material from a actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material as published here was seat ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention in putting these commentaries side by side is to compare the approaches of the different schools in order to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice.]

The Therapist Writes

This man, a Roman Catholic priest in his early forties, came into therapy for three slated reasons: to cope with his feelings about his father's death; to explore his roots, cultural, familial and religious; and to ‘have the experience of therapy’.

The material in this report has been disguised to preserve confidentiality.

The History

He comes from an extremely enmeshed family. Father was fifteen years older than mother and, though a devout Roman Catholic, had already been divorced. His sister is twelve years older than himself, born before his parents were married. The family are Anglo-Asians, who lived in Africa, but came to England to escape political troubles when he was nine. The family considered England to be their homeland and suffered a great shock when their joint fantasy of living in ‘a cottage in the country’ was destroyed by their first sight of the two-roomed flat in a Liverpool tenement which was to be their home for the next seven years. They never spoke of their disappointment with each other. The whole family shared one bed until he was seventeen, but he did not think this abnormal until later. He has no recollection of any possibility of sexual relationship between his parents and finds the thought of it ‘rather distasteful’ - his father would have been a ‘dirty old man’. His father was ‘always old’, treated by mother more as uncle or grandfather rather than husband. He has had no sexual relationship, nor any admitted desire for one.

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary by an Analytical Psychologist (and Family/Marital Therapist)

Moira Duckworth

Moira Duckworth

Moira Duckworth  

In writing this I find I have been unsure if I should confine my comments to those which would more naturally be used if I were supervising this work, or if I should try to comment from a stance of imagining myself as the therapist. These two overlap, but supervision quite clearly takes place with the existing framework of the therapist and patient and what is contained in that. When supervising, I hear of many things done and said which I might well not do or say myself, but I have to look and see if it is appropriate to the situation being presented. What I might have done in the same situation may or may not be relevant. My personality and psyche is not the therapist's personality and psyche or vice versa.

Writing about this case proved more difficult from the alternative interpretative viewpoint, which has felt like an intrusion into the work. It is possible that my counter transference is picking up either the feelings of an enmeshed family when the rigid boundary between themselves and the outside world is threatened, or the feelings of an outsider trying to negotiate that boundary. Maybe at some level that might reflect the feelings of the therapist in this case.

I am interested in the stated reasons for seeking therapy: (1) ‘To cope (my emphasis) with his feelings about his father's death’. Coping has for me an air of maintaining the status quo and somewhere this speaks into one of my feelings about this case - that it could be stuck (though I do not deny it is also moving) around father. Where is mother? (2) ‘To explore his roots … etc.’ Identity is the word which springs to mind. There is an identity crisis - and no wonder! This man hardly exists as an individual. (3) ‘To have the experience of therapy’, i.e., to have an experience he has never had. Is this where mother comes in? I'm sure that is not what the patient consciously intended. I note that he is in his forties, and think of mid-life crisis and Jung's ‘second half of life’. Coming from an enmeshed family and being firmly established in Mother Church, he is likely to be very resistant and frightened. I would want to find a way of relating to the fear.

The fourth Rugby Psychotherapy conference was held at Herbert Gray College on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, 11th, 12th and 13th January. We began after dinner on the Friday with two personal statements of the essential ingredients of psychotherapy, one given by Elspeth Morley and one by John Davies.

Although I had to guillotine the discussion that followed, it was continued throughout the next day and on into the Sunday and meshed in very nicely with the Saturday morning clinical demonstrations which had been particularly asked for at the 1984 Conference. We offered a social work ease done as a fishbowl which was a supervision session, a guided fantasy and a video demonstration of sexual marital therapy.

After a coffee break, there was a session conducted by a humanistic psychotherapist, a demonstration of hypno-therapy and a repeat of a video demonstration. These produced a great deal of interest and lively discussion. There was a break from lunch until tea, and in that time a meeting of ‘psychodynamic organizations’ was held, which had been announced at lunchtime by its convenor, on whether or not they had a collective view about the question of a directory, an agenda item for discussion on Saturday evening. I did not go to that meeting, feeling that, as Chairman, I really had to look after the interests of all represented organisations and instead I had a well-earned nap. I understood at teatime that most of the Conference participants had, in fact, gone either to participate or to observe.

After tea, we gathered together for a briefing on the development of the training document, the ethics document and the question of the directory from Shirley Wade, who has been collating the information we have been collecting year by year. responseSet.title: Femininity Grows Up
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Femininity Grows Up

Sir,

I would like to comment on the papers in your first issue by Joan Raphael-Leff and Andrew Samuels. While Samuels provides an illuminating survey of Jungian thinking which can easily be related to other theories, I think Raphael-Leff fails in her stated aim of clarification. She sets out to dispel myths about motherhood, but by introducing categories of her own she is more likely to become known as the perpetrator of a new myth. The challenging of existing theories is only significant if the author has something better to offer. A bald statement that the maternal instinct has not been proved does not constitute progress.

The depressing truth is that we still lack a satisfactory concept of femininity. Many people think Freud's concept of penis-envy is a non-starter as a basis for a psychology of women, however useful it may be clinically. What has been lost sight of in post-Freudian thinking is the clear distinction Freud made between infantile sexuality and adult genitality. The difference between small-boy assertiveness and the responsible potency of the adult man is perfectly obvious. The same distinction could be made in female behaviour but I have not come across it. There is a real risk that the strident assertion of pseudo-independence by feminists will influence a whole generation of young women into accepting an infantile phallic role for lack of affirmation of their basic experience of themselves as women.

Samuel's paper comes as a refreshing experience after Raphael-Leff's, providing clear statements about individuation. Jungians have an advantage over Freudians in the fact that Jung always stressed the importance of the whole person. I would like to connect Jung's schemata of the personality with Freud's concept of adult genitality as alternative ways of describing the goals of life. Samuels shows that Jung's schemata are not concrete entities but dynamic concepts describing the interplay of different aspects of the personality. The myths described by RaphaelLeff are based on over-simplification and downgrading of the ideas of various authors. We need a concept of wholeness which can embrace the different dimensions active/passive, receptive/assertive, thinking/feeling, etc. On this basis Raphael-Leff's choices seem to me misconceived and without relevance to the integrity of the personality.

What is unusual in a blind supervision is the fact that both therapist and patient, as well as the quality of the session, are unknown. Bearing this in mind, I will focus on two aspects, not necessarily in this order: 1) the material which is being presented, and its meaning in the here-and-now; and 2) the therapist's countertransference.

lust before the session, the therapist notes ‘I became aware that there was something of an insatiable child within this powerful father …’. The session then starts. The first associations are in fact an insatiable demand upon the therapist, who understands the ‘accusations’ and starts wondering if he is asking too much. I would not question the patient on this point, because he is not interested in it; he is interested, I think, in sorting out his internal reality first.

The patient is expressing depressive (and persecutory) anxieties, linked in this moment with the interval between sessions (or the weekend) ‘he left the last session feeling dismayed, and he has been feeling the same ever since’.

The interpretation could start from the self-reproaches and include the description of the therapist as a bad object, something on the line of ‘… in my absence have been present in your mind as a reproaching, tormenting voice’.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Language of Psychotherapy: Metaphor, Ambiguity, Wholeness

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

London WC1E 6AU

Jeremy Holmes  

Summary

Psychoanalysis is approached from the perspective of linguistics. It is argued hat analysis is concerned with a type of communication different in nature and logic from that of the natural sciences. The characteristics of analytic language are illustrated by comparing poetry and psychoanalysis. Transference is discussed as a special type of metaphor; ambiguity is seen as an intrinsic aspect of aesthetic language; wholeness is held to be a goal of both therapy and the arts. The relevance of this view to recent findings in neurophysiology and ethology is discussed.

Introduction

Psychoanalysis has two faces. One is public, outer, claiming a place in the mainstream of scientific-rational medical culture. The other is the reverse: private, inner, courting the arts rather than the sciences, but conscious as it does so that this may, by the procrustean rules of our cultural divide, disqualify its outer aspirations. This ambiguity has internal and external repercussions. Critics have seized on the outer surface of psychoanalysis and sought to show that it does not measure up to the rigorous standards expected of a true science. Farrell (1981), for example, in a recent book, invokes a psychology of common-sense like Jane Austen's as an antidote to Freudian metapsychology. Psychoanalysts and their supporters often feel confused by this miscomprehension and have been tempted to retreat into their esoteric world, claiming as they do so that critics such as Farrell, with little direct analytic experience, have missed the point. They might, before disappearing into their consulting rooms, also remark that it is the very breakdown of commonsense solutions to their problems that drives people to seek help; that what we call ‘common-sense’ is a complex and mature psychological state, one certainly not possessed by infants and small children; and that Freud's stated aim of therapy, ‘where it is, there ego shall be’, might be seen precisely as an attempt to replace the uncommon and unbridled sensation of neurosis with the common-sense of normality.

Family Therapy: Concepts and Methods by Michael Nichols Published by Gardner Press: New York 1984; 609 pp.; £27.50.

E. Andrew MA

E. Andrew

London

E. Andrew  

For three decades of its existence, family therapy has been, in Lynn Hoffman's words, ‘an endeavour in search of a theory’. In few other disciplines would it have been possible for a student to choose among so many different schools, each claiming to offer unique insights for their brand of therapy. Partly this springs from the fact that family therapy is struggling to contain two totally opposite epistemologies. One developed from the theoretical ideas of Freudian psychoanalysis, was linked with classical scientific models, presumed a linear causality and focused on the individual and his intrapsychic processes. The other stemmed from the work of those who had been influenced by modern mathematical and biological sciences and is linked with developments in communications theory and computer technology. It includes work in general systems theory, in cybernetics and in information theory. It considers the individual and his environment as a system, interlocking within a series of interrelated biological and sociological systems influenced by a circular causality.

This initial split became prominent in the seventies with the development of schools of family therapy; the literature reflected the mood. Practitioners rushed into print. Some books, like Minuchin's Families and Family Therapy or Haley's Problem-solving Therapy became classics in the field. Other important contributions were the collections of papers, like those of Guerin (1976) or Paolino and McCrady (1978). But it is a psychologist, Michael Nichols, a student of family therapy in many settings, who is the first to attempt a comprehensive review of the whole field from its earliest days. Undeterred by ‘an apparently chaotic development that incorporates conflicting and contradictory points of view’ (page 3) he seeks throughout to illuminate the underlying principles that bind, rather than divide, the differing schools. And this is not all; along with the main history, he includes parallel developments in adjoining disciplines, like Moreno's work in psychodrama or Bion's group dynamics.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychotherapy with an E.S.N. Head-hanker

Robin Balbernie

Robin Balbernie

Robin Balbernie  

My heart sank as I surveyed the pair in front of me. This was one of my first referrals at a new post; and I was well aware that my growing, decsion to try to work with this child stemmed more from the wish to get on and do something than from any real conviction that I could help. His mother was doing all the talking at me, listing her complaints in a harsh staccato voice which gave the impression that she took time to sharpen each sentence before hurling it forth. Her son, Joe, was never given the chance to say anything for himself. About all lie did manage was, at the end, to stammer out that he would like to come to see me. This clinched it to make a start, and somehow suggested that there was hope after all.

‘The neighbours all get at me because he never stops banging his head. They'd be happy if I got up a petition to have him put away. They all pick on him, and all the kids, too. They say he's a raving loony. The next door comes round and complains because they can hear him banging on the wall’. As she rattled off her accusations, Joe goggled at a point about three feet above my head and shifted about uncomfortably in his seat. If I asked him anything, he looked horrified, and could manage no more than a mumbled ‘yes’ or ‘no’ as a counterpoint to his mother's almost instant interjection.

Joe, it seemed, had begun head-banging just before he was two years old. This had continued unabated up until now when, at the age of thirteen and a half, he was attending the local delicate school. They had requested a psychiatric assessment as it was felt that things were generally going wrong for him. He was bunking off more frequently, which was not surprising as when he did attend he was regularly bullied. When this happened, his mother said, he returned home ‘in a mood’ and banged his head against a wall.

He was finding it hard to get to sleep of late. When he was at home his favourite pastime was playing with his vast collection of toy cars, on which he spent all his pocket money. He would often wander about pretending to be a car himself; another reason why, according to mother, ‘All our estate say he's a raving nutter’.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary

(In this section a short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material as published here was sent ‘blind’ to two people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention in putting these commentaries side by side is to compare the approaches of the different schools in order to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice).

Clinical Commentary III

The therapist writes:

The Patients Personal Background

The patient is a 29 nine year old man, divorced and now involved with a woman who is in England for a limited period of time taking a course. He is highly successful in a difficult profession and his present job and workplace are particularly competitive and emotionally bruising.

He was born abroad and when his parents returned to England he was seven years old. His personal care reverted abruptly back to his mother from servants. He remembers the transition as one from relative indulgence to a noticeably stricter regime. From this time on he had a repetitive dream in which he was searching in busy streets for his parents, spotted them, chased them, finally caught up with the couple who turned and revealed they were strangers.

At first his father was the bete noir in therapy, described as puritanical, moralistic and harsh. But it soon seemed, to me at least, that while he was at least involved with the patient, the mother was not. The patient described his mother's care as cold and mechanical. However he is in the present much involved with her and visits her regularly. His father died some years ago. He has one sibling.

In therapy he described attacks and injuries to his self esteem in childhood. These took the form of teasing by other boys which left him undermined. He later wondered whether he really had been teased so badly, or whether great harm really had been intended by other boys. He went to a public school - though his parents were not well off - which is well known for its tough regime. There were no homosexual incidents, or so it is claimed.

Commentary by an Independent Psychoanalyst

Sharon Steklman

Sharon Steklman

Sharon Steklman  

There are many difficulties involved in commenting on a short written clinical account. Many questions must remain unanswered and one is obliged to contain one's speculations.

For myself I view the transference as a re-enactment of the patient's internalised relationships between the subject and objects and therefore the nature of the actual transference - who is the therapist representing and, indeed, who is the patient representing - is a question that I keep very much in mind at all times. The countertransference, too, is an invaluable guide in orientating oneself in the expressed internalised relationships.

In the case of this young man his relationships are described as scourging. It seems to me that it is the patient's objects that are felt by him to possess everything, but which are ungiving and dismissive and that he can only acquire anything tot himself by a process of reflection from them.

Correspondence

Brett Kohr

Brett Kohr

Oxford OXl 4JF

Brett Kohr  

Sir,

Psycho-Analysis in Orford: A Study in Heresy'

In the early twelfth century, a group of theologians gave birth to the University of Oxford. The University motto, Dominus, iltuminatio meo', still in use today, serve, as a reminder of its religious infancy. During adolescence, the University offered instruction in such topics as sin, heresy and eternal damnation; most of the dons were cleric. Such a catholic upbringing, brimming with spiritual indoctrination, will inevitably produce an obsessional personality unable to tolerate doubt or creative imagination. And as the University never received any psychotherapy during its life-cycle, the neurotic character structure became more heavily reinforced and defended. When psycho-analysis, that distinctly Jewish profession, first appeared in England, the University became highly suspicious and immediately protected itself by establishing an institute of psychology where ‘scientists’ could study the behaviour of rats. And when David Astor offered a substantial sum of money to the University to establish a Professorship of Freudian Psychology, the University officials scoffed, and proceeded to develop a department of psychiatry dedicated to the administration of drugs and electroconvulsive shock treatment, and a department of clinical psychology skilled in the fine points of systematic desensitisation.

In 1982, I felt starved; my alma mater did not nurture me, and I found myself commuting to London several times a week just to hear psycho-analytical lectures. In 1983, 1 rebelled, and with the aid of a group of psycho-analytical enthusiasts, we formed the Oxford Psycho-Analytical Forum. Dr. Muriel Gardiner generously accepted our offer to serve as the Inaugural Lecturer, and with over one hundred people in attendance, we began in earnest to provide for the needs of our abandoned siblings. (Dr. Gardiner spoke on some of the technical differences between Viennese psycho-analysis of the 1920, and contemporary psycho-analysis. To the best of my knowledge, this was Dr. Gardiner's last public appearance before her unfortunate death).

S. Lieberman MD F.R.C. Psych.

S. Lieberman

London S. W. 1

S. Lieberman  

This is a book about two Hans. The Vienna Hans was a little boy afraid of horses. He became one of the most celebrated of phobics as proof of the childhood sexuality theory of Professor Fernald. The Berlin Hans was a Horse. He was not afraid of little boys. He was thought to be the most erudite of horses, the Einstein of quadrupeds. Alas, scientific observations led to his unmasking. Berlin Hans' major talent was that of detecting the headnods of his questioners.

On the one Hans the story proceeds as a scientific detective story with observation followed by hypothesis, followed by construction of experiment, followed by results. Results lead to fresh hypotheses and further experimentation, Such was the way in which the horse's lack of wits were unmasked.

On the other Hans, the story proceeds as a search for the proof of a theory. It is a compellingly human quest for meaning in symptoms. How the search proceeds, and why the particular meaning falls nicely into line with the infant theory of child sexuality, is a tale which provides the clasp between the two Hans.

Hans the child grew up to be a relatively normal man who shunned publicity. Hans the horse advanced along a road of public acclaim despite having been exposed. What lesson can be learnt from these two famous Hans? Why does the author juxtapose them?

The book is dedicated to the theme of investigator effects. Fernald reveals all on page 214:

Pfungst and Freud as investigators, Clever and Little Hans as subjects, and Mr. von Osten and Little Hans' father as unwitting culprits, all played a role in demonstrating various investigator effects. The old schoolmaster's subtle signals were discovered by the experimental method. The parent's subtle signals were observed in the clinical method. Both studies show the potential for errors not only through cueing but also in observation and interpretation. Control of these factors is a constant problem in science, and it has been recognised as a special problem in psychology since the early days of Clever and Little Hans.

Commentary by an Analytical Psychologist

Christopher Perry.

Christopher Perry.

Christopher Perry.  

Reading through this session, I was struck again and again by a lifeless quality both in the material and in the patient's response to his therapist's interventions. The lifelessness, together with the history, led me to the following tentative formulation. The patient is a twenty-nine year old man who has survived repeated experiences of rejection, separation and loss throughout his childhood and adolescence by developing a do-it-yourself approach to life and by functioning mainly in his head. His ego strength is manifested in his capacity to hold down a highly competitive job and to control and manipulate others; but the ego is also deformed in so far as the patient cannot relate. Relatedness or giros has been replaced in him by a ruthless power, just as his deep wish to opt out for a more relaxing and supportive way of life seems to have been defended against by his striving at work. The history and treatment background are peppered with the language of sadomasochism -‘bruising’, ‘scourging’, ‘touch regime’, ‘harsh’, ‘violently rejected’ - reflecting, I imagine, a kind of transference, countertransference dynamic in which the patient is barricading himself up against the therapist, exerting maximal control and recreating the cold, mechanical ambience of the mother-infant relationship.

The patient believes that he can only be brought alive from outside, possibly by anal rape (e.g. ‘need a lot of stimulus from without’), but I wonder whether the anality is a smokescreen for a deep longing and hunger. The patient says ‘What you say has no impact’, implying that the feeding experience with the therapist is simply a physiological event, denuded of imagination and emotion. This may be because the patient is stuck at the negative pole of the archetypal great mother, in so far as that image has not been mediated or humanised by a good-enough actual mother. Perhaps this rift between the archetypal and the human is reflected slightly in the reporting, which at two points suddenly goes into the third person, hinting to me that the therapist is being coerced into incarnating the ‘cold, mechanical’ mother. The repetitive dream links in here because of the patient's lifelong search for loving parents, a search that brought him into analysis, in and out of marriage, and now towards a notion of emigrating. Is this last a flight from dependence on the therapist, or is it also a hopeful regression to incest with the mother in order to be reborn and so move on developmentally?

Y. Parker  

The assumption of innate knowledge of classical psychoanalytical concepts and the use of jargon render most textbooks on psychotherapy almost unintelligible to the novice. Richard Parry's book provides a refreshing and stimulating entry to this world. Well written and easy to read, it is lightened by humorous insight into the discrepancy sometimes found between the ‘ideal’ and the actual practice of therapy. Aspiring therapists will recognise with some relief that even experienced colleagues are liable to similar pitfalls and difficulties.

The goals and likely limitations of therapy are clearly outlined and illustrated by examples in the early chapters of the book. As an anxious apprentice I particularly appreciated the practical advice concerning establishing a therapeutic relationship. The ‘sea. t’ of what the therapist actually says or does is often avoided by other texts and mysteriously withheld by tutors.

Medical students, general practitioners and trainee therapists alike will find this book invaluable in demystifying a complex subject and instilling the confidence to explore a rewarding area of clinical practice.

Reality and Reason: Dialectic and the Theory of Knowledge by Sean Sayers. Published by Basil Blackwell, Oxford, 1985; 224 pp; £19.50 hardback and £7.50 paperback.

David Will

David Will

David Will  

Sean Sayers' book is something of a tour de force. It provides an extremely clear account of some central areas in the theory of knowledge and forcibly develops a realist account of knowledge. For Sayers, knowledge is always a reflection - albeit a complex and mediated one - of reality. He defends this view against its traditional opponents such as idealism (the idea that knowledge is merely a construct of ideas and interpretations) and relativism (the idea that all knowledge is merely socially constructed and therefore relative).

The blurb outlines some of the book's central issues as follows: ‘Is knowledge a reflection of reality? What role do experience and interpretation play in knowledge? Can truth be objective or is it socially constructed and relative?’

In answer to these questions, Sayers develops the thesis that all ideas - including false, illusory and irrational ones - reflect objective reality. Why should these questions be of interest to psychotherapists? The history of psychotherapy is littered with examples of what happens if idealist or relativist ideas become fashionable. Like it or not, every psychotherapist confronts such issues in everyday clinical work.

A recent example of idealism at play in our field, is Lacanian psychoanalysis, where it is held that we can never know anything about ‘the Real’ but, rather, are always only dealing with linguistic codes or the illusions of the Imaginary.

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Two articles in this issue are on the psychotherapy of children. They come from very different areas of work, but raise similar questions. Robin Balbernie reports a brave attempt to tackle the unpromising - an ESN head-banger. He confides that his reasons were spurious and require an apology. Such an apologetic stance seemed to fit with the patient's own assessment of himself. The outcome was that odd paradox, in which optimism comes from sticking with the sense of defeat and hopelessness. In view of the good outcome, were the reasons for taking on the case as spurious as the author implies? What are valid reasons? And what countertransference feelings should a psychotherapist allow himself to be persuaded by?

Dean Eyreinvestigates several points of intervention. He begins by countering the claim that the hyperactive child has suffered brain damage. In his paper he shows that the child is ‘damaged’ by maternal depression or anxiety. Interestingly he reports both a child who is hyperactive and an adult who was hyperactive as a child. He concludes that once it is realised that the maternal problem needs investigation, it is possible to offer brief psychotherapy by taking the mother's own difficulties seriously. He has found that this point of intervention can afford rapid relief of the child's problems. Here is a confident assertion about the most favourable point of intervention, and it is backed by the evidence of solid clinical work - work with the mother rather than the child.

How confidently can we take another psychotherapist's conclusions? Inevitably this Journal is thrown back to pondering differences between different approaches.

Jeremy Holmes' article extends Rycroft's view of psychoanalysis as a theory of semantics, a biological theory of meaning. He distinguishes two modes of mental activity which might be employed by psychotherapists. We may think scientifically about the object of our interest as a material mechanism; or we may attempt to engage with our patient as a personal subject. We are currently familiar with the debate that Bettelheim has raised over Freud's position. Traditionally, Freud was thought to have reluctantly traversed a road from hard-nosed scientific determinism to a more ‘soft-nosed’ humanistic psychology. But Bettelheim has claimed that this is an artefact of the English translation, made in the context of a scientific establishment in the English-speaking world, and that Freud was much more concerned with his patients as human people. (The counter-claim is also possible: that Freud was a hard-nosed scientist who had to put his psychological discoveries into the animistic and anthropomorphic style of the German philosophical tradition).

Gertrud Mander PHD

Gertrud Mander

Westminster Pastoral Foundation

Gertrud Mander  

This book starts from a concept, personal responsibility, which the author, a Stanford-trained Counselling Psychologist recently emigrated to Australia, considers a first principle and defines as ‘the process of making the choices that maximise an individual's happiness and fulfilment’. ‘Focussing on personal responsibility,’ he writes, ‘is almost like focussing on one's nose.’ He makes a qualification, however, and insists that his ‘integrative approach’ which intends to bridge the gap between the humanist and the behaviourist approach, between the counsellors who believe in persons, self-awareness and meaning, and those who focus on actions, skills, and learning theories, is only tailored to ‘ordinary people, not to the moderately to severely disturbed populations’. Focussing on the noses of the latter will thus require other methods which are not mentioned. Nor is the reader told how to tell ‘ordinary people’ from the others.

If I sound critical, this is because the author's commonsense psychologist manner and the prescriptive-didactic tone of the book exude an easy optimism, which the counsellor whose work is more concerned with the excluded categories of the client populations cannot share. There are, to be fair, some fundamental areas of overlap, where Nelson-Jones' eclectic approach agrees with the psychodynamic and analytical approach which is deliberately excluded from the pool of ideas he draws on. He stresses empathic listening, for instance, puts an emphasis on meaning, on experiencing feelings, and dismantling self-protective thinking habits.

Dentition: A Fundamental Element in Normal and Pathological Development (the Correlation between Normal and Pathological Structure)

Adriano Giannotti and Giuliana De Astis

Giuliana De Astis

Department of Child Psychotherapy - Instituto di Ncuropsichiatria Infantile University of Rome

Giuliana De Astis  

We have elsewhere (Giannotti, De Astis 1979; Giannotti, De Astis, Catarci 1982) examined aspects of early developmental processes in the child on the basis of clinical material from psychotherapeutic work on structured cases of autism and childhood psychosis.

We paid special attention to the role of the birth experience, the mother-child relationship and to drives - in particular the oral-aggressive drive, as it emerges during dentition. In this paper, we shall consider and elaborate that theme, drawing out its implications for the autistic pathological structure and giving clinical examples.

Reflections on Early Childhood Development and Role of Cutting Teeth

On the basis of clinical experience, we intend to stress the fact that problems and difficulties related to dentition are a fundamental element of normal and pathological development.

Early dentition covers a period from approximately six to 30 months, reaching its culmination most often around the period immediately preceding deambulation. It therefore covers a good part of childhood development, and the way its bodily, symbolic, affective, aggressive and destructive meanings are integrated is strictly dependent on preceding experiences and on the quality of early environment.

Briefly to summarize psychic development, especially as far as emotional and affective difficulties are concerned, we recall the normal autistic phase (Mahler 1969) which occurs in the first weeks of life, when the child satisfies his need and experiences his first emotions mainly at a bodily level through his omnipotent autistic activities. At this stage, the child's libidinal cathexis and the bodily experiences which result from it are predominantly oriented towards enteroceptive stimuli, while the mother helps relieve excessive stimulation, both internal and external, by acting essentially as a protective shield (Masud Khan 1963).

Most recent studies on the newborn baby (Brazelton 1980) based on direct infant-observation confirm how early the suckling child learns to use his innate capacity for attention to discriminate selectively between external stimuli (maternal voice, physical contact, sight) which foster a state of homeostasis and integration, while being able to eliminate selectively negative stimuli.

responseSet.title: Freud Soulved
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Freud Soulved

Sir,

Dr. Lieberman, in his review of Bettelheim's Freud and Man's Soul, (British Journal of Psychotherapy Vol. 1, No. 1) says ‘After reading this book 1, for one, will be able to approach Freud's work with less distaste for its distancing technicalities.’ I suggest that his apparent blanket acceptance of the work leaves many very complex questions in obscurity. Let me confine myself to some problems of translation.

We may agree that such words as ‘cathexis’ and ‘parapraxis’ are unedifying importations into English which has its own words -‘investment’, ‘faulty achievement’ -that will do the job better. I does not follow, though, that all Bettelheim's suggestions about translation can be so easily accepted. ‘The Ego’ and ‘The. Id’ do indeed sound strange and technical to the man on the Clapham omnibus; but I am assured that Das Ich and ‘Das Es’ sound equally strange to his German equivalent - certainly my linguistic eyebrows raise themselves at ‘The I’. In any case, this is not simply a matter of substituting one word for another; there is a broader question of how we talk about psychic structure. ‘Where it was I shall be’ sounds fine; yet it doesn't help, any more than did its predecessor, with where we fit in the unconscious ego.

Finally the rendering of ‘Seele’ presents a higher order of difficulty. ‘Mind’ is certainly wrong; but despite Bettelheim's claim ‘soul’ will not do either, since it has inescapable non-materialist connotations which ‘Seele’ lacks. And if there is one thing that we can all agree on it is that Freud, whatever his stand on humanism, stood to the end for a materialist psychology. (For what it's worth, my own suggestion is that until something better turns up we duck the problem by using ‘psyche’.)

Bettelheim's book raises many important issues. But I have too frequently found its assault on medicalisation being used as ammunition by those who wish to remove sexuality from its central place in psychoanalysis. Bettelheim is a serious writer who deserves a more intelligent and less uncritical response.

responseSet.title: An Open Letter to David Will
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

An Open Letter to David Will

Sir,

In his criticism of the Maudsley School and the Anti-Psychiatric movement David Will characterises these antithetical approaches as both sharing the same positivistic epistomological presuppositions. Consequently, he claims that these schools mirror each other in their theoretical practice, ‘demarcate areas of forbidden knowledge, conflate epistemology and ontology, and deny that reasons can be causes’. Will indicates that Transcendental Realism will overcome the unproductive distortions of this matching pair. However through an implicit claiming of a spurious scientific neutrality his article betrays a close endorsement of the medicalisation of psychotherapeutic concerns, and a grave misunderstanding of AntiPsychiatry, which is merely a way station within a much wider discursive order.

The Medicalisation of Psychotherapeutic Concerns

Firstly there is a quite explicit privileging of the Maudsley School at the expense of the Anti-Psychiatric movement whilst claiming that they are merely opposite sides of the same positivistic coin. Will wishes ‘to make it clear that [he is] in no way disputing that in certain areas e.g., epidemiology and psychopharmacology, the Maudsley School has made an undoubted contribution to psychiatric knowledge’. As this was never in dispute and given that there is no such explicit endorsement of the anti-psychiatric contribution, one is left with the indelible impression of moving towards the ultimate absurdity that, for example, Leff and Wing's 1968 study of ‘the use of phenothiazines in the treatment of schizophrenia’ has made a greater impact on the understanding of psychosis than the work of R. D. Laing.

Secondly there is explicit endorsement of the theory of the hereditary basis of mental illness. Here Will gets himself in quite extraordinary tangles and exhibits instances of just that which he criticises: conflation and double pleading. There is conflation of evidence and proof: he endorses ‘…clear evidence [of] organic/ genetic factors of aetiological significance in schizophrenia…’ This may be evidence but it is not proof. Why is it not possible to argue that the Heston and Kety's adoption studies merely show that ‘organic/genetic factors’ are sufficient (in those cases) but not necessarily present in every instance of diagnosed schizophrenia rather than, as Will does, the other way round?

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Two and a Half Cheers

Sir,

Congratulations on the first edition of the new Journal.

The clinical commentary was fascinating with each of the discussants raising interesting points on the case presented. Yet, regardless of the different theoretical perspectives which emphasize various aspects of the case and particularly of the

224

patient's psychopathology and experience, I notice a significant similarity in the comments on the therapist's input; ‘… the almost compulsive interrupting style the therapist found himself adopting’ (Samuels, p. 81); ‘The therapist's irritation and impatience is evident in dealing with the patient during this session’ (Boutall, p. 85); ‘It is, as we are shown, very difficult not to react with impatience and in that way get caught up in acting out the active role in the relationship’ (Jackson, p. 88).

I hope this is evidence of a basic agreement on the importance of fully conceptualising the interactive nature of the therapeutic relationship, and I wonder if I could add a few words about the therapist's contribution to the communicative network developed by both patient and therapist in this session because perhaps it ultimately gets less attention than the patient's. It is important, for example, that in the summary of the previous session to that reported, only the patient's communications are given. Should we assume the therapist was silent? Probably not, because this would very much contradict the style commented on so unanimously in the reported session. We do know that the therapist felt pushed out and ignored (‘very little space or attention for my interpretations’) and had been told by the patient that his symptoms had returned ‘which by implication was a very disheartening occurrence’. To whom - only the patient, as implied? Eventually the general complaint about ‘the way analysts talked’ is voiced. So the patient is calling attention to precisely the issue noticed by all three commentators.

I would imagine that this therapist might have been feeling angry, ignored, under pressure or certainly uncomfortable, and maybe Samuels' suggestion that we look at the shadow and the subjective dimension could usefully be applied to Boutall's sample interpretation to help us understand more about this therapy.

Supervision of the Therapeutic Large Group

G. P. Pullen

G. P. Pullen

Oxford

G. P. Pullen  

The “Oxford Large Group Study Group” has regularly discussed the large groups taking place in seven local psychiatric facilities. Psychodynamic and other anthropological concepts have proved of value in attempting to understand the complex events presented, with the central role of the “theme” being confirmed. The extension of psychotherapy supervision to the large group appears to have been of value to the study group's members and may also have helped the participating units.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Models of Meditation

Michael Delmonte and Vincent Kenny

Vincent Kenny

James's Hospital, Dublin 8

1 James's Street. Dublin 8

Vincent Kenny  

Experiential aspects of the more common forms of meditation,, described in the context of some research findings. Various theoretical models of meditation are reviewed. Meditation is also discussed in terms of behavioural, psychoanalytical and personal construct perspectives. It is concluded that whereas no simple or singular conceptualisation of meditation is adequate, personal construct theory has most to offer in describing meditation phenomena. The objectives of the various meditation techniques appear to be rather similar, i.e., to achieve insight into the workings of the mind, selfmastery, and ultimately to transcend the ego. However, meditation experiences may vary considerably within and between individuals.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Salomon Resnik dwells on the meaning of crisis as a moment of truth. He is concerned to distinguish the positive aspects of crisis from catastrophes. And indeed he makes the point that his therapeutic endeavour is to help the psychotic to make the distinction between these two experiences, because it is part of psychotic life to anticipate catastrophe as a part of every intrapsychic change.

Marco Chiesa describes pregnancy similarly as a crisis, one that threatens some extreme distress. In the case he presents, the catastrophe has a form, unlike the raw and ungraspable sense of catastrophe that Resnick discovers in his psychotics. The pregnant woman uses the foetus inside as an internal object that makes concrete the worst fears about dangerous internal objects. Chiesa showed that, because of the focus of crisis in the limited period of pregnancy, it was possible to conduct an effective therapy in a similarly time-limited period. For the pregnant woman, the evidence of the actual object inside her is almost a realisation of the actually unthinkable.

The actually unthinkable does sometimes in fact occur in external reality. Monica Lanyado describes two children who were subjected to actual experiences of this kind. She describes the critical counter-transference helplessness, and the need to meet this with a containing ‘maternal reverie’.

Herbert Hahn delineates the concepts of transference and counter-transference from a theoretical point of view and a Kleinian perspective. He then illustrates with clinical material selected from three separate settings, an analytical psychotherapy, student counselling and career guidance. He shows that attention to the therapist/counsellor's awareness of the atmosphere (counter-transference) in each setting is central to understanding the problem.

The model of the counter-transference as a container for the transference is taken up by myself from the patient's point of view. The activity of the therapist is assessed by the patient in terms of the therapist's ability to contain him. Much has been written about what is therapeutic in analysis and psychotherapy, and what is the intrinsic nature of the therapeutic intepretation. Through looking at mistakes, one can turn the question around and ask what is anti-therapeutic about incorrect interpretations.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Commentary by an Eclectic Psychoanalytical Psychotherapist

Robert Royston

Robert Royston

Robert Royston  

There are many workable approaches to a session. I find particularly useful one which concentrates on the form, on what the statements of both protagonists do and are, rather than on what they say. The form of the session, what the patient does, is often a type of enactment of unconscious themes. An understanding of form also quickly attacks resistance and is, I think, appropriate to the patient discussed here, whom I take to be in a phase of grudging engagement in the work of exploration.

At one point in the session discussed here, for example, the patient suddenly praises the therapist and predicts a marvellous cure. This comes after gloomy complaints about lack of progress and after opening comments to the general effect that the previous session was so discouraging as to be almost damaging. I suspect the praise is a reward to the therapist for his recent comment about the patient showing feeling in the session, a comment which rescinds the criticism passed in the last session.

The patient's praise, or so it appears, is accompanied by a rush of excitement. It embodies what I think R. Langs would call an offer of a misalliance, a nonanalytic ‘cure’ aimed at sealing off the pathology of both protagonists. The patient is saying the therapist's usual method will never effect a cure. He, the patient, just hasn't the puff. The therapy is not only damaging him, but the therapist too. A wise, good man he may be, but his adherence to the psychotherapy organisation and to analytic rules has turned him into a sadistic machine. And yet, the patient implies, were the therapist to ditch analytic psychotherapy something really exciting could happen. There would be a cure. The patient's keyhole could be spied through and the real material would be on show. The therapist too might find himself able to reveal himself as a person to the patient.

This attempted seduction, if successful, would have afforded the patient aggressive satisfaction. It would also excite him with the prospect of ‘sinful’ anti-analytic exchanges with the therapist. And, the misalliance successfully forged, all pathology would be sealed off from investigation. Is it too far fetched, too, to wonder whether the patient, a religious man, is also unwittingly trying to introduce nonanalytic types of emotional help he may have heard of through pastoral counselling: co-counselling, for example, or befriending, as practised by the Samaritans?

[[RunningHead]]

The Hyperactive Child: A Psycho-Analytical Approach to Theory and Treatment

Dean Eyre

Dean Eyre

161 Waverley Street, Ottawa, Ontario K2P 0W4, Canada

Dean Eyre  

At times in our work we are faced with symptoms in our patients which, because of their complexity, seem to defy understanding or treatment. Driven by our own frustrations at not being able to find an easy answer, we cope with the problem by reifying it and describe the symptoms instead as a syndrome, further defining and qualifying the situations that it occurs under including or excluding data which either support or detract from the syndrome complex that we have discovered. Child psychiatry, by its very nature, has had more than its share of these syndromes and the one I wish to focus on is, as stated in the title of this paper, the hyperactive child. Without by any means describing a comprehensive list of causative agents for the syndrome, almost everything has been invoked from food additives and allergies to minimal, otherwise undiagnosable, brain damage. In this paper I will put forward the hypothesis that the hyperactive child is a visible symptom of a latent disturbance, a disturbance of, and distortion in, the mother-child relationship. I will attempt to support this hypothesis with reference to work by, among others, Balint, Laing and Winnicott, with clinical material from the analysis of a three year old child who was hyperactive and from the analysis of a 30 year old woman who was hyperactive as a child. I will then attempt to show by reference to case material that, using this hypothesis, brief intervention along these lines can quickly change the overt clinical presentation.

Laing (1959), in his work on family dynamics and interaction, showed how a member of the family can be designated as ill, to protect the mental health of the family and often one particular member of the family. In this process, unwanted and unacceptable feelings and affects are projected into the scapegoat who is then subjected to the family hostility and rejection. The victim, for his part, acts the ill or disturbed person that he has unconsciously at first and then later consciously been designated. The mental stability of the family is maintained. With the alteration in the mental status of the scapegoat an imbalance or instability sets in with the rest of the family. Likewise, terms used to describe the wrongs of the scapegoat can seem, at times, quite extraordinary to an outsider.

Psychogenesis: The Early Development of Gender Identity by Elizabeth Moberly Published by Routledge and Kegan Paul: London 1983; 87 pp.; hardback £9.95.

B. K. Fowles A.A.P.S.W.

B. K. Fowles

London

B. K. Fowles  

In this book Dr. Moberly has produced a new hypothesis concerning the psychodynamics of homosexuality and of transsexuality. This states that the condition is not caused, as has been believed, by close attachment and identification with the parent of the opposite sex, but by an earlier detachment and disidentification from the same sex parent, as a result of early trauma.

It is an attractive theory, especially since it seems to offer the opportunity for providing in therapy a later reparative relationship with a same sex therapist which could lead to further growth into heterosexuality, but Dr. Moberly, although she has put a great deal of work into her thesis, produces no real evidence for her case. Added to a book of only eighty seven pages she has more than twenty closely-printed pages of bibliographical references, but her use of all these largely consists of criticisms of the theories and findings of other writers, whose statements she rejects. Emphatically she repeats her own statement over and over again, whilst giving no results of her own research, nor any illustrations from cases in point. True, the first chapter concerns Freud's case of Schreber, written in 1911, but this example, perhaps by now out-dated, seems slim evidence on which to base a revolutionary new theory. I would have liked Dr. Moberly to have shared the content of her research programme with us. In the light of the lack of material her case comes across largely as dogma.

I found myself confused too by her arguments concerning damage produced by the father, a secondary love object; less so, of course, by that caused by the primary love-object, the mother. Indeed at one point, on p. 79, she sets out at some length the familiar case for preventing maternal deprivation, having talked a great deal of the male homosexual's loss of father, which seems not quite to fit her case.

Surely there are exceptions to her thesis which we may have met, like the homosexual son of a deserting mother and a maternally caring single parent but masculine father. I was also driven back to my own belief that gender identity confusion arises not from rejection of the one parent and thereby being driven too closely to the other, but by the conflict between the two parents, so that true identification cannot be obtained from either. The girl rejecting her mother dare not get too close to her father, and if the boy rejects his father his closeness to his mother may result in identification crisis. It is inevitably neither one or other parent; it is the situation with both, resulting in a triad. It is more complex than Dr. Moberly seems to make it.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychology and Freudian Theory: An Introduction by Paul Kline Published by University Paperbacks, Methuen, London, 1984; 177 pp; £11.95 hardback, £4.95 paperback.

John Denford

John Denford

John Denford  

The intention of the author is to give an introduction to psychoanalytical theory and its status in relation to modern psychology, for ‘students and non-specialists’. There are clear and generally satisfactory summaries of basic Freudian theories, followed by a discussion of some of the objections which have been made to them, and of some solutions. Then follow five chapters detailing experimental psychological investigations which have sought to test the validity of the main categories of psychoanalytic theory: child development, oedipus and castration complexes, dreaming, the nature of the unconscious. Then comes a discussion of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy, and of the general psychological and social implications of the theory, and a brief useful statement of conclusions.

For a student who knows little of psychoanalysis, the summaries of theory should give a reliable panoramic view of the subject without bogging him down in details and developments which he should only come to gradually, through wider reading. For someone who is familiar with the subject, they are adequate but suffer in the way summaries often do, by seeming bald, over-definite and not qualified or illuminated by the detailed explication and clinical illustrations which make them more real and convincing. On occasion one is left thinking ‘is that really what I understand, or believe?’ and, after further thought, forced to agree that ‘indeed it is’ - not an uncommon experience when one hears non-analytic scientists propound psychoanalysis. Perhaps something in the clinical experience modifies the concepts, subtly and consistently.

Paul Kline is Reader in Psychometrics at the University of Exeter, and has published many psychological studies of Freudian theory. His attitude to psychoanalysis is clearly sympathetic but his sympathy is tempered by experimental psychological attitudes and assumptions. He argues convincingly that psychoanalytic theory consists of a series of hypotheses (or inspired hunches) about human development and behaviour, which can be (and in some cases have been) tested in suitably designed experiments. The chapters that form the centre of the book contain reasonably detailed accounts of the main experimental evidence that has been gathered so far, to support or refute the hypotheses of psychoanalysis.

To make attractive to the average person; make easily acceptable or understandable’, so the Dictionary defines the task of the popularizer. The popularizer, I would add, should successfully appeal to the intellect and intuition and stop short of spoon-feeding.

In spite of all the difficulties involved there is, I think, a resurgence of interest in Psychoanalysis, and a real desire to know what it can and cannot offer, what it does and does not claim… What I intend to do in this book is to explain to the general reader some of the ideas and discoveries which have arisen out of the work of analysts, particularly in England, over the last 50 years or so.

The question is: can we explain that which is experiental at its very core and essence without our readers throwing up barricades of fresh resistance, even if we may succeed in mitigating earlier ones? The writer tells us that her chief influences have been Klein, Bion, Segal and Rosenfeld. We know the fine stable of this mare. But Bion had a lot to say about Analysis as Transformation, concerning the quintessence of moving from K to O, where K is knowing about and O the truth we can become. The minute that we write ‘about’, the question instantly arises, do we write from K or O, for without the latter enzyme the former may not be digested.

Julia Segal's interest in Psychoanalysis, we are told, ‘has “been fed” by a personal analysis, by courses and seminars at the Tavistock…. and work supervision from several senior psychoanalysts.’ My own experience of her book was that it offers us a painstaking and comprehensive display of all this first rate nourishment, which at times moves just a little close to a regurgitation.

What shall we do with the Drunken Sailor?

Maurice White

Maurice White

London W12

Maurice White  

Here in the Annexe, a small therapeutic community inside a top security prison, we are at the very soul of the human condition. Hate, violence and contempt mingle with extraordinary compassion and sympathy. Now in our thirteenth year, we exist to offer an alternative, especially for sexual offenders, to isolation and inevitable reinforcement of the perverse attitudes that pose such a threat to society.

I do not intend to offer a statistical assessment or even a conventional clinical description of this Unit. Instead, I will endeavour to convey some measure of the intrinsic meaning of our work and its relevance, not only for the inmates under our care, but also for the community at large. In an age when the terrorist and the Mafia loom large, we must concern ourselves with a search for a framework that will help us grapple with such evil forces, in all their guises.

However, the meaning of our work goes beyond ‘treating’ the criminal. At the same time as we explore ‘their perversions’, we meet our own. An essential ingredient of our work is to examine the social structure of the hierarchy, i.e., the Staff and Institution attitudes. Too often we see the veil of respectability being used as a cloak to perpetuate evil. The Headmaster, Child-care Worker, Scoutmaster or Father who beats the bottom of his charges, and while ostensibly rubbing in cream to ease the pain of the wounds, buggers the child. Many of these figures initially start from a mental attitude of saving the victim from wrongdoing. The Murderer who pours scalding water on the Sex Offender feels he is avenging wrongdoing, and can experience an elated sense of self-righteousness and the congratulations of his friends for his actions; surely enough to make those of us with experience in the field have strong reservations about the simplistic notion of the ‘short, sharp shock.’

A View of the Patient

In order to convey the understanding of what dominates the mind of a typical offender in our Unit, I will give a few brief extracts which I hope will communicate the nature of their fantasies and mental states. Then I will turn to some of the attitudes which dominate the structures we establish in reacting to these pressures.

A rationale is offered for the use of homework assignments in brief therapy. The little boy wants to kill his mother so as to have his mother all to himself. The little girl attempts to push her mother away so as to enjoy her father on her own. This is the oedipus complex, generally accepted as inevitable, even normal. The terminology, however, has not been chosen at random: a complex is a symptom pointing to an illness (depression-neurosis-psychosis) which needs treatment. George Dubai, a psychoanalyst from Geneva has put the cat among the pigeons by asking: why accept the fatality of the oedipus complex which gives so much pain to humanity? Dubai attacks the taboo ….with a plea for love.

Ordinarily a pamphlet comprising one paper reprinted (with a change of title) from the Journal of Psychology and Theology together with a Brief Response written by the Administrative Secretary of the Clinical Theology Association might not have merited notice among the book reviews. But the Association evidently proposes a series of Lingdale Papers; as in this case, they will no doubt deal with the interface between psychotherapy or counselling and the Christian faith.

Such writing must be tested in the terms of the quality of its theology, of its psychotherapeutic content and of its treatment of their integration. Benner's theology, tactfully modified by Peter van de Kasteele in his Response, rests upon a substitutionary account of the atonement; his unsatisfactory use of object relations theory includes the proposition that one of the basic curative factors in psychotherapy is ‘…to encourage the patient to put inner confusion and chaos on to the therapist…’ (nothing here about mirroring or the withdrawal of projection); and the relationship between them lies in a parallel concerning the unconditional acceptance of the badness of others.

These reviewers believe this kind of cross-disciplinary enterprise to be valuable in principle. However, perhaps inevitably because of its brevity, the present example is superficial and - in encouraging counsellors to be simply persistent receptacles in the name of Therapeutic Love - seriously misleading. We must hope for better things later in the series.

Dr. Herman's book is so absorbing that once started it becomes difficult to put down. There is something compelling and gripping about the way we are allowed to participate in the innermost struggle of a person's determination to fight for life: the purpose of the struggle the emergence of a separate identity.

This book is an unusual kind of autobiography - it leads the reader through the gradual unfolding of an anaytical process with the unique connotation of the personal experience of an individual. However, at the same time offering with it a degree of universality.

In his article on autobiography (T.L.S. May, 1983), Dr. Rycroft says: “My own ideal conception of an autobiography is one in which the autobiographer remains in pursuit of himself while recounting himself.” This is indeed the impression one gets in the reading of “My Kleinian Home” - a trip of “at-onement” in Bion's sense as Kavafi's beautiful poem Ithaka at the beginning of the book indicates. The focus of the book is not on the actual life-events and interactions with other people, but on the forging of meaning that unifies one life and thereby creates a sense of personal identity. How this meaning is attained is conveyed to the reader both through a direct emotional impact and a reflective conceptualisation of its underlying structure.

Brief Focal Psychotherapy with a Pregnant Woman Presenting with Nightmares of Killing Her Baby: A Case Study

Marco Chiesa

Marco Chiesa

Marco Chiesa  

Introduction

This paper is about an 18 session, brief focal psychotherapy with a five month pregnant woman, previously infertile, who suffered from an intense anxiety state and depression following horrific nightmares of murdering her yet unborn baby. This case confirms what D. Pines (1982) wrote in her paper, ‘My analytic experience has led me to believe that there is a marked distinction between the wish to become pregnant, and the wish to bring a live child into the world and become a mother’. In the case of the patient I am going to describe, a tremendous hostility towards her own mother and a conscious wish to become pregnant were linked with unconscious fears that if she were to become a mother, she would hate her child enough to kill him.

The working through in the transference of her hostility and resentment towards her mother and the analysis of anxieties of a persecutory nature allowed an amelioration of the clinical picture and the avoidance of a likely puerperal illness of some severity.

The experience of pregnancy reactivates conflicts unresolved in previous deve lopmental stages and the temporary regression to a primary identification with one's own mother may bring about primitive fears of merging with her, with a consequent threat of loss of identity. In the patient I shall be talking about, early separation from her own mother determined a partial failure of self/object differentiation and the increase of primary hatred and hostility. After she became pregnant, the inevitable regressive identification with a hated mother produced loss of boundaries with consequent confusion; through projective identification, she felt she was at the same time her own mother, herself and the foetus she was carrying.

Primitive anxieties of merging and losing one's identity, and uncontainable hatred and guilt, become remarkably accessible in these patients and deep interpretations can be made from the very first session. Indeed, with less disturbed pregnant women, one or two therapeutic consultations have been reported to be an adequate intervention. This paper shows how brief psychotherapy could be useful also with patients who present with deep-seated pathology and with a history of early deprivation, provided high motivation for insight and willingness to become deeply involved in the therapeutic relationship are present on the patient's part.

On Learning from the Patient by Patrick Casement. Published by Tavistock Publications, 1985; 244 pp; £6.50 paperback.

Andrew Cockburn

Andrew Cockburn

Andrew Cockburn  

The dust jacket of this book carries an intriguing illustration of an empty chair and couch placed close together. The chair is tilted towards the couch; one of its legs looks like an extension from it. Underlying both is a black shadow which, though irregular and blurred in outline, is continuous. By contrast, the couch and chair, whilst separate, appear joined up by the underlying shadow. It is as if there is a kind of dialogue going on, thus depicting the interactional nature of psychotherapy - the principal theme of this book.

What has prompted Casement to write it is to rescue psychoanalytic insights from becoming cliché-ridden, and to enhance and promote our creative learning from patients. This is coupled with a wish that those in caring professions, as well as analysts and therapists, be encouraged to ‘play with’ the ideas put forward and not to feel excluded, as many do, by the esoteric language in which many specialists in the unconscious speak to each other. In the first paragraph of his introduction, Casement refers to the dilemma of student therapists. One of the noteworthy features of this book is the way in which the position and special needs of students and inexperienced therapists are continually being addressed.

An essential part of Casement's thesis is set out in Chapter 2: The Internal Supervisor. This was written after the clinical material comprising chapters 3, 5, 7 and 9, and represents a formulation of one of the prime issues in psychotherapy, namely how to be psychologically intimate with a patient and yet separate. Following Winnicott, Casement invokes the notion of a nursing triad: that is, of the mother who is emotionally held while she holds the baby. The passage is worth quoting:

As with the mother, this holding of the student therapist is first experienced as coming from outside. Transitionally the experience of supervision is usually internalised. Ultimately this needs to develop into an internal support that is autonomous and separate from the internalized supervisor…. It is a function of the internal supervisor to hold the therapist who is learning to hold the patient. This provides the structure of an internal ‘nursing triad’ which can help the therapist to find an inner play-space where the clinical options can be explored.

Loss and Internalisation

Jonathan Pedder

Jonathan Pedder

London, S.H.5

Jonathan Pedder  

Introduction

A previous paper (Pedder, 1982) reviewed psychoanalytic concepts of depression, starting with Freud's classic paper Mourning and Melancholia, then Kleinian views of the depressive position and Winnicott's re-naming of this concept as the stage of concern. Also considered from a psychoanalytic viewpoint was the work of Brown and Harris (1978) on the social origins of depression and particular attention was given both to their finding that loss of mother before the age of eleven predisposes women to depression and to the links between this phenomenon and the development of self esteem.

This paper is an attempt to look again at the essence of the ideas I was trying to bring together there and to focus on those that need further exploration.

Background

Although the concept of the depressive position has been a seminal one in psychoanalytic circles, it does not seem to have passed into the general body of psychiatric thinking in quite the same way as have, for example, the original psychoanalytic concepts of defence mechanisms.

In Segal's words (1964) ‘The depressive position has been defined by Melanie Klein as that phase of development in which the infant recognises a whole object and relates himself to this object’ (p.55). This central idea turns up again and again in different language: that a crucial stage occurs in infant development when other people are recognised as separate individuals. Recognising mother as a whole person, the source of good and bad experiences, heralds the depressive position and the realisation by the infant that his own destructive impulses may harm the object that he both loves and totally depends on.

Winnicott (1962), in writing of similar phenomena, chose to speak of the capacity for concern in order to emphasize the positive, rather than the negative, side of the same experiences, i.e. that the infant is beginning to care about and feel responsible for what happens to the object. He felt the term depressive position to be a bad name because it did not emphasize sufficiently the achievement of this stage.
