The Patient's Defensive Analyst

R. D. Hinshelwood

R. D. Hinshelwood

R. D. Hinshelwood  

Psycho-analysts and psychotherapists do not always make correct interpretations. It is a difficult technique. Probably all of us make mistakes quite often. I shall argue that this is a very complex event - more than is commonly recognised. When it happens it needs close analysis in the session.

Part of the complexity derives from the emotional work the analyst must do in recognising the situation, and which is avoided more often than is commonly recognised. He has to overcome his own narcissistic wishes - a task which will not escape his patient's attention.

It is therefore complex because ‘the analyst who made a mistake’ is a figure who plays a significant part in the transference and counter-transference. He is an object of great emotional meaning for both patient and analyst. I shall present material to show that the ‘analyst who made a mistake’ is experienced by the patient as an analyst who is defensive.

A further bit of the complexity is that the patient may believe insistently that the analyst is mistaken, even when he is not. At such a moment the patient is divorced from the reality of his internal and external relations. This requires the same emotional work from the analyst to recognise that he is being perceived as an ‘analyst who has made a mistake’. And if the analyst is hesitant or resistant to recognise it, he does indeed make a mistake that confirms his patient's view of him.

From the patient's point of view, the ‘analyst who made a mistake’ and the ‘analyst who is being perceived as having made a mistake’ are one and the same. In this paper I shall not distinguish between the two as I shall be sticking closely to the patient's experience. For the patient, he has a defensive analyst whose priority is to protect his own mind. If the patient detects a defensiveness, real or imagined, how will he understand it?

The Analyst's Mental State

As the concept of transference has developed, the emphasis on the psychopathology of the patient and on the analyst's interpretive precision has given way to the examination of the interaction between the patient's transference and the analyst's interpretations. This change has followed the realisation that patients make a very close examination of the analyst's mind through his interpretations. Some patients' exquisite sensitivity to the analyst's state of mind dominates the whole of the day to day activity in sessions.

Internalization in Narcissism: The Problem of Disillusionment

Robert May

Robert May

30 Johnson Chapel, Amherst College, Amherst, MA 01002, USA

Robert May  

One of the areas of liveliest interest, and controversy, in American psychoanalysis over the last fifteen years has been that of narcissism. (For the purposes of this paper I include both psychoanalysis proper and the adjoining field of psychoanalytic psychotherapy). The two major voices have been those of Otto Kernberg (1974) and Heinz Kohut (1977). Each has constructed an extensive theory of how the narcissistic aspect of human character develops, what is internally amiss in serious narcissistic difficulties and what therapeutic strategies are best calculated to put it right.

It is intriguing that this debate, often boisterous at close range, has had few reverberations in Britain or Europe. One could put this down to the inevitable national parochialism which plagues psychoanalysis, or to the ways in which narcissism seems a quintessentially American concern and is less culturally, and thus clinically, prominent elsewhere. But also important, it seems to me, is the way in which Kernberg and Kohut represent attempts, complex and useful attempts, to introduce into American ego psychology some theoretical and technical emphases which are already familiar in the British school of psychoanalysis.

Kernberg is forthright about his debt to the work of Melanie Klein and he has laboured quite effectively to integrate some Kleinian notions into American ego psychology (this has been done in the face of what has often seemed a ritual reflex of denigrating Klein on the part of American analysts). Both by connecting Kleinian concepts to the developmental and structural theory of ego psychology and by writing about it all in the precise and objectified style which has characterized the classical theory in America, he has detoxified and made respectable an important set of ideas. The Kleinian aspect of Kernberg comprises, to take just the major elements: an emphasis on early mother-child relationships (two person and “pre-Oedipal” rather than triangular); a belief in the importance and primacy of envy and hostility; and an emphasis on the central role of fantasy, internal objects and primitive splitting in the internal world (note the similarities between Kernberg's theory of narcissism and Rosenfeld's 1964 paper).

K. P. Fink MD FRC Psych

K. P. Fink

K. P. Fink  

This book is addressed to the general public and Robert Langs tries to update Freud's Psychopathology of Everday Lie, The Interpretation of Dreams and The Joke and Its Relation to the Unconscious, plus some other writings.

Fangs is a populariser of psychodynamics and a prolific writer who is author and editor of many books and is an indefatigable promulgator of the understanding of the unconscious. His seminars and workshops are well known and well attended.

In Unconscious Communication in Everyday Life he explains the layers and levels of meanings contained in everyday communications. The book is divided into 19 chapters and numerous sub-sections and Langs attempts to go step by step in explaining how every communication, however banal it may seem, has a meaning and what kind of meaning. He carefully classifies people into senders and receivers of messages and then into people who send true messages and those who send false messages; he also says that receivers can be true receivers or false or lie receivers. He gives numerous examples, some of which seem a bit superficial at times, but they are in fact addressed to the very lay reader and are intended to be as didactic as possible. Langs spends a great deal of time in explaining how to understand the meaning of communications, that is, in his words, how to decode the encoded meaning. He applies this same system to dreams and emphasizes that the trigger (that is, the reason for sending a communication or for having a dream) is the basic fact that has to be understood.

The hook is addressed to the lay public and I would say also to beginners in psychodynamic studies. The language is very clear, although some people will object to the usage of English that Langs makes in order to clarify his thought and the wary he derives a series of terms of the basic word ‘code’. The book is worthwhile reading and having for professional and semi-professional people. Beginners will benifit from it and probably acquire some new communication skills.

Surviving Trauma - Dilemmas in the Psychotherapy of Traumatised Children

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado  

Introduction

It is a sad fact that some children have had such terrible life experiences that their parents feel that it is beyond their own resources to help them recover, and so they decide to seek professional help. The children have become isolated, and totally different, from other children. They have actually experienced what is felt to be unthinkable and unbearable by their family and the community at large. As a result they have become emotional ‘untouchables’.

In this paper I would like to share the dilemmas experienced in the therapy of two children who have suffered in this way. The first child, nine year old Lesley, was referred to me five weeks after she had been raped with full penetration, not far from her home, whilst walking the dog with a friend. She had been a ‘normal’, lively child before this happened. When I first met her, she was tragically shocked, as indeed were her family and the local community from which the alleged rapist came. The other child, Derek, was also nine when he was referred to me. He was not, in fact, referred because of his past traumatic experience, but because he was stealing and behaving extremely dangerously, as if he believed he was a ‘cat with nine lives’. However, I was told by his adoptive parents at referral, that he may have witnessed the murder of his natural mother by her lover when he was two and a half years old. Paradoxically, they also assured me that he really knew nothing about what had happened in his past or why he had been adopted.

For both of these children, I was immediately aware of my gut reaction of horror at what they had experienced. I found it difficult to be genuinely emotionally available to them in the transference. This holding back on my part, I realised, was similar to the reaction they felt they generally evoked from adults around them. In particular, a gulf existed between them and their parents in which the traumatic event appeared to block close emotional contact at a time when this was desperately needed.

Cecilia Clementel-Jones

Cecilia Clementel-Jones  

psychotherapy, pregnancy, pregnant psychotherapist.

The reactions of individual psychotherapy patients and colleagues to the first pregnancy of the author are discussed within the framework of the limited literature available. The associations to the pregnancy theme in both staff groups and therapy groups are discussed. The view is put forward that evident avoidance of this area of clinical observation in the literature is linked to a need to defend an outdated view of analytic neutrality.

Transference and Counter-Transference in Practice

Herbert Hahn

Herbert Hahn

Herbert Hahn  

Summary

This paper looks at some psycho-analytic definitions of transference and counter-transference, notes aspects of the wider application of these concepts and offers three examples from professional practice which relate to the theme.

Transference

Freud on Transference

Transference is the English translation of Freud's term Ubertragung. (Langenscheidt New Concise German Dictionary definition: ‘Assignment (of rights), delegation (of powers), transmission (radio), spreading (disease)’). Freud first saw transference as a form of resistance, later as a powerful therapeutic tool. He mentioned it initially in 1895 as a manifestation of the patient's resistance against insight, then developed in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) the theory that transference is part of our psychic functioning by which unconscious impulses find expression in our dreams. In his clinical paper on his patient Dora (1905), he finally introduces the notion that transference is the central factor in the therapeutic process: he says that transference refers to the ‘series of psychological experiences’ which are ‘revived, not as belonging to the past, but as referring to the therapist at the present moment’. Treatment does not create transference but brings it to light. It is an ‘inevitable necessity’ in treatment, and only after the transference ‘has been resolved’ does the patient gain ‘a sense of conviction of the validity of the connections which have been constructed’ during the therapy. In his paper The Dynamics of Transference (1912), Freud states: ‘In each individual as a result of the interaction of hereditary and environmental influences, what might be described as a stereotype plate’ is produced (or several such) ‘which is constantly repeated - constantly reprinted afresh - in the course of the person's life, so far as the external circumstances and the nature of the love objects accessible permit, and which is certainly not entirely insusceptible to change in the face of recent experiences.

The Narcissistic and Borderline Disorders by James F. Masterson Published by Brunncr/Mazel: New York 1981; 246 pp; £26, hardback.

Martin Village

Martin Village

Martin Village  

There is a spirited debate in progress on the other side of the Atlantic and it concerns the origins of narcissistic psychopathology. Dr. Masterson's corner in an ideological cosmos which includes such luminaries as Kohut, Kernberg, Spitz and Winnicott (with a nod in the direction of his true and false self) is secured by his espousal of what he calls ‘confrontive psychotherapy’ as a technique in the treatment of borderline patients. His present contribution is aimed at making a theoretical distinction between borderline patients and narcissists (something which he says Kohut failed to do) and then to illustrate with case histories the considerations of technique which flow from that distinction.

Doubtless we have not heard the last word from this author on the matter of the developmental theory which underpins his technique. It has been criticized as being simplistic (Kernberg) but it also manages, simultaneously and without paradox, to be complicated. We are introduced to a world of WORU's (Withdrawing Object Relations part-Units) and WORU's (Rewarding Object Relations part-Units) which the borderline patient acts out in the transference; while the narcissist is afflicted with equally unpleasant ‘defensive, grandiose, omnipotent, self-object fused-units’ or ‘underlying, empty, aggressive fused-units’ which he acts out in his transference. Rather suspiciously, Dr. Masterson's developmental theory seems to provide all the answers, at least in the case of the borderline patient. All, that is, except one: the developmental arrest of the narcissistic disorder can occur before that of the borderline, and yet in psychoanalytical terms the problems of the borderline patient are much more severe. Why?

In matters of technique this author has much to offer the practising therapist in diagnosing and treating pre-oedipally disturbed patients. He suggests a systematic analysis of narcissistic patients' grandiosity rather than collusion with their tendency to idealize the therapist (which he suggests was Kohut's approach). And in the case of borderline patients his confrontive psychotherapy comes into its own. Rather than ask the interpretative ‘why?’, the borderline patient should be confronted with his own destructiveness, and the therapist should be saying to him ‘Look what you're doing to yourself’. Central to the confrontive technique is the idea that borderline patients cannot form transference bonds in the normal way and are not susceptible to interpretations. What they indulge in is ‘transference acting out’ which is essentially a defensive posture and must be confronted by the therapist in his assault on the so-called ‘Borderline Triad’ of separation/individuation, abandonment depression and self-destructive defensive behaviour.

Art as Therapy. An Introduction to the Use of Art as a Therapeutic Technique Ed. by Tessa Dalley Published by Tavistock Publications, 1984; £13.50 hardback, £6.95 paperback.

Dorothy Judd

Dorothy Judd

Dorothy Judd  

Art therapy was established, through a hard struggle, comparatively recently in this country, as a recognised therapy with a professional training. The term was not used until the 1940s and criteria for training were really only established in the 1970s. The post-graduate training for art therapists now has DHSS approval, and combines clinical and theoretical studies, the application of the therapist's own creative side and the development of self-awareness.

This book conveys a wide range of views on art therapy, in theory and practice. It is addressed to a wide audience, in related professions, as well as to ‘those who basically believe that there is more to art than paint on paper’. The editor, Tessa Dalley, defines art activity as generally having a therapeutic purpose, but makes the distinction between art aimed at looking good, and art where the process of creation is of primary importance. She describes art activity undertaken in a therapeutic setting, in the presence of a therapist, where the ‘art activity provides a concrete rather than verbal medium through which a person can achieve both conscious and unconscious expression, and can be used as a valuable agent for therapeutic change’.

She then attempts to consider what makes art therapeutic, as not all art activity is healing. She describes the value of using symbolic representation in art, rather than in speech, when speech is impaired, under-developed, or rejected as the normal means of communication. Making marks can be a fundamental and universal means of communication - ‘even for the most articulate, art can be used as a type of “symbolic speech”, a means of saying something non-verbally through symbols’. She adds that symbolising feelings and experiences in images can render them less threatening. I feel that although this could be a valid view, it implies that verbal expression is more threatening than visual expression. This assumption is also made elsewhere in the book, and is the sort of generalisation which is perhaps meaningless without the backing of clinical material. From my own experience of psychoanalytic psychotherapy, that which is expressed verbally in the therapy room equally has the opportunity of being transformed by the therapist from what might be ‘nameless dread’, or Beta elements (Bion), into something that can be thought about.

[[RunningHead]]

The Psychotic Crisis

Salomon Resnik

Salomon Resnik

Salomon Resnik  

In Greek Hippocratic medicine the term ‘crisis’ was used to indicate the ‘climax of the illness’, a critical point determining the subsequent course of the disease process towards a favourable outcome or a worsening condition. The Greek word KRINEIN from which the word ‘crisis’ derives carries with it the idea of separation, of a tear which will lead to a decisive transformation. That is why, in the individual or social history of man, it has always implied a radical change, marked by what we call a ‘moment of truth’.

In the course of long experience with psychotic and non-psychotic patients, I have been able to confirm the hypothesis that a crisis is always, for good or evil, a moment of clarity. Rudolf Otto (1969) described the religious crisis as a ‘luminous’ experience taking the space and name of the divinity - ‘I am the light’, ‘I am God’.

Kant (1781) used the concept of ‘the critical point’ to indicate the process by which reason looks into itself. Thus criticism is an experience of reason questioning itself. Later Husserl (1954) treated the topic of crisis from a phenomenological and social point of view. For Hegel, criticism is connected to knowledge and to the fact that all attempts at knowledge imply a risk. Marx, influenced by Hegel, described alienation as a ‘crisis of regulation’. In his writing on alienation Marx (1867) traced the degradation of work to the effect of reducing man himself to a commodity. The reification of work, making it into a thing, leads to the reification of man himself (Lukacs 1922). The relationship between man and the objects in the world becomes a common focus of interest for political sociology and for psychoanalysis. The feeling of impoverishment of the ego in the psychotic patient approximates to the sense of alienation that men feel in their work, when they excessively project their energy and creativity into the good they produce only to find they disappear with, as it were, their own psychic capital. Hinshelwood (1983) has examined this correspondence between the processes of alienation and of projective identification.

Envy Loveth Not: A Study of the Origin, Influence and Confluence of Envy and Narcissism

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

41, Weston Park, London N.8

Joseph Berke  

Envy is an inborn, destructive motivating force, opposed to love and antagonistic to life. Writing in The Metaphysic of Morals in 1797 Immanuel Kant had no qualms about describing envy as ‘the vice of human hate’, a moral incongruity that delights in misfortune (Schadenfreude) and ingratitude. He called envy a ‘hate that is the complete opposite of human love’ and concluded:

The impulse for envy is thus inherent in the nature of man, and only its manifestation makes of it an abominable vice, a passion not only distressing and tormenting to the subject, but intent on the destruction of the happiness of others, and one that is opposed to man's duty towards himself as towards other people (Kant, p. 316).

Over a hundred years later Freud also commented on a hatred which opposes love. This is a hatred which is directed against ‘any source of unpleasurable feeling’ including the absence of something needed; the presence of noxious sensations; and over-excitement, an intolerable inner tension associated with the very things a person wants.

The ego hates, abhors and pursues with intent to destroy all objects which are a source of unpleasurable feeling for it, without taking into account whether they mean a frustration of sexual satisfaction or of the satisfaction of self-preservative needs (Freud 1915, p. 138).

Mere relief from the distress does not assuage such a degree of unpleasure. On the contrary, it remains as a passionate hostility towards any stimulation, even rooted in desire, which has become too painful to bear. Freud said this was a hatred ‘older than love’ (1915, p. 139). His description fits a rudimentary envy which averts love and transforms intense interest and excited desire into malevolence.

Desire and dislike are manifest in specific physical and psychic activities from birth. The infant ingests, inhales, takes in all that he needs and wants. He evacuates, expels, puts out whatever he doesn't need and dislikes. The psychic equivalent of taking in is introjection, and of putting out is projection. Both the physical and psychic processes are means by which he interacts with the ‘world’ - everything going on in and around himself.

Listening as a Four-Level Activity

John Rowan

John Rowan

79 Pembroke Road, Walthamstow Village, London E17 9BB

John Rowan  

This theoretical paper argues that there are many isolated insights offered by practising psychotherapists which would be more usable if they were integrated into a suitable model which would relate them are to another. A model is offered which distingushes between four levels of the person: body, feelings, intellect and soul or spirit. This model is used to examine four types of listening found in the literature: empathy, awareness, counter-transference and resonance. It is shown that what this is done much more coherence is found, and it is then possible to talk in terms of holistic listening. A set of diagrams is developed which suit the model and make it more teachable.

Some implications are drawn out to, the education of psychotherapists. In, curd, in psychotherapy and for the selection of psychotherapists by potential clients.

To our surprise a person may come out of a depression stronger, wiser and more stable than before he or she went into it.

Winnicott (1964, p. 126)

Self-preservation for modern man means keeping the symbolic self intact. Fundamentally this involves his being able to receive and process messages accurately, and to understand and orient himself to their significance.

Basch (1975, p. 528)

Clinical and ethological conviction that discrete affect expressions are adaptive and that they represent an early and continuing significant form of communication has received experimental support.

Emde (1980, p. 78)

Introduction

This paper describes how certain behaviour patterns tend to prevent affect and process of depression from facilitating adaptation. Its point of departure is the position that the capacity to respond to specific circumstances with the affect of depression is not only universal but adaptive unless unfavourable events during the most formative years have interfered with normal personality development.

In general, with some exceptions in psychoanalytic literature and in multidisciplinary research as reported by Izard (1972), the study of clinical depression often lacks this point of view which is more readily applied to other categories of emotional disturbance. Wanton destructiveness, for instance, is recognized as a consequence of faulty personality development or of other damaging influences that distort the expression of a vital normal affect. Sexual deviation is also seen as a consequence of a development that interferes with the course of a vital normal function. In contrast, symptoms of clinical depression are rarely measured against any model of normal depression. The question how and when depression serves an indispensable adaptive function and therefore is a sign of normal development is not raised. Thus, there is no general agreement on such a model, although Freud and/or Klein are often assumed to have provided one.
